title: A fossil-competitive primary supply of multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated industrial process that uses CO2 as its carbon feedstock, water as its hydrogen source, and low-carbon energy to make a named multicarbon chemical at a cost competitive with its fossil-derived counterpart. Ethylene is the principal demonstrated chemical example in the supplied evidence. The target is a dependable primary supply of useful material, encompassing conversion, carbon recovery, purification and sustained production.

Multicarbon products contain two or more carbon atoms, so producing them from CO2 requires building carbon–carbon bonds as well as reducing the carbon feedstock. The supplied ethylene study demonstrates this chemical conversion in the laboratory. The proposed breakthrough would carry that capability through a complete production system whose energy use, carbon efficiency, durability, equipment requirements and product quality support competitive operation.

Scope synthesis: the concept is defined by the feedstocks, named product and integrated performance, rather than by a mandatory single reactor architecture. Direct electrochemical conversion and routes involving intermediate products could both qualify if the complete process met the same requirements. Success for ethylene would establish a supply route for ethylene; it would not automatically establish competitive production of other chemicals or liquid fuels.

significance.text: A competitive CO2-to-ethylene process would create an alternative carbon supply for an existing industrial product. The revolutionary change would lie in how the product is supplied: carbon that currently enters production through fossil feedstocks could instead enter through captured CO2. The reported laboratory conversion establishes a chemical basis for this conditional possibility, but does not establish its industrial competitiveness.

Conditional impact synthesis: wider adoption could reduce geological-carbon dependence in plastics, solvents and fuels, provided suitable product-specific processes were developed and deployed. That outcome also depends on the CO2 source. Reusing CO2 captured from a fossil-derived stream alone would not establish independence from geological carbon. A credible climate benefit would additionally require low-carbon energy and accounting for capture, conversion, purification and the product's eventual use or disposal.

The analogy to solar hydrogen has an important limit. Hydrogen production can provide an enabling input for some chemical routes, but it does not itself supply carbon-containing products or demonstrate carbon–carbon bond formation. The supplied outdoor hydrogen efficiency reports therefore illustrate progress in a related energy-conversion capability. Their different efficiency conventions and heating boundaries also prevent treating their percentages as a directly comparable progression toward multicarbon production.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied demonstrations is an integrated production system that combines selective conversion with competitive total performance. High faradaic efficiency means a large fraction of electrical charge produces the desired product; it does not, by itself, establish low electricity consumption, high utilization of incoming CO2, inexpensive purification or low production cost. These quantities must be reconciled across the complete process.

Concrete engineering barriers include maintaining product selectivity and useful current density over long operation, providing sufficient electrode area at acceptable cost, recovering carbon from process streams, and separating the desired product without erasing the conversion advantage. Pressure management must also be evaluated across the system. The ethylene study's energy argument concerns using captured CO2 at its existing pressure rather than first depressurizing and later repressurizing it; it does not establish that high pressure generally minimizes total energy consumption.

The economic barrier remains distinct from the laboratory chemistry. The reviewed supplementary analysis models a 100-tonne-per-day ethylene factory with a 20-year life and optimistic capital-cost assumptions, including the electrolyzer and pressure-swing adsorption unit. Such modeling can identify conditions under which a process might become attractive, but measured operation must establish whether conversion, separation, equipment life and auxiliary requirements can satisfy those conditions together.

Assessment boundary: the supplied evidence does not demonstrate the complete target. It also does not establish that no qualifying system exists anywhere as of 2026-11-01. The remaining breakthrough described here is the gap between the supplied achievements and the concept's integrated requirements; worldwide present-day absence remains unresolved.

current_state.text: Huang, Gao, Zhao and colleagues, published in Nature Catalysis on 28 August 2025, report up to 85% faradaic efficiency and an ethylene partial current density of 750 mA cm−2 at 20 bar. They also report stable electrolysis for more than 1,500 hours at 600 mA cm−2 and a proof-of-concept product stream brought to 99.9% ethylene purity. These are substantial laboratory achievements. The reported duration is roughly two months; the supplied account does not establish that every peak performance figure and the purification result were maintained together throughout that run.

The ethylene main article was available to the supplied review as a partial subscription preview containing the abstract, while the complete matching supplementary information was available. The supplement extends the evidence beyond the original abstract-only description and distinguishes laboratory separation work from projected factory economics. Its 100-tonne-per-day economic scenario is a model under optimistic assumptions, not an operating plant demonstration. Likewise, the energy conclusion addresses avoiding a depressurization–repressurization cycle for already pressurized captured CO2; it does not show achieved commodity displacement or a general minimum-energy operating pressure.

For hydrogen production, Zhang and colleagues' Science Advances paper, published on 26 February 2025, reports outdoor solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies of 29.1% at 95 mA cm−2 and 25.9% at 240 mA cm−2 in a photovoltaic–alkaline-electrolysis system. The supplied review had an identity-verified full article through an alternative-hosted PDF. It records external heating used to emulate heat that could be available in a larger system, and an efficiency calculation using a 1.23 V convention. These details qualify the interpretation of the reported efficiencies as complete-system energy performance.

A 2026 Communications Engineering paper by Martínez, Ohlmann, Smolinka and Dimroth reports an outdoor peak solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 31.3% for a Fraunhofer concentrator module. According to the full publisher PDF described in the supplied review, that figure uses hydrogen's higher heating value and excludes energy for preheating water to 60 °C. Improved thermal integration is proposed for a future design. The result therefore has a different accounting boundary from the Zhang study and should not be read as an unqualified efficiency improvement over it. Neither hydrogen experiment demonstrates multicarbon chemical production.

Evidence boundary: the supplied texts do not document the originally asserted complete photovoltaic–electrolyzer–syngas pilot chains or establish their deployment status. That evidentiary gap does not show that such chains do not exist. The supplied freshness-search record is empty, so these dated achievements cannot establish an exhaustive worldwide state of the field on 2026-11-01.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration milestone: continuously produce ethylene or a named liquid fuel from CO2 and water at tonne-per-day scale for thousands of hours, with measured output quality and independently checked energy and carbon balances. Report throughput, electrode area, operating pressure, durability, maintenance, auxiliary inputs and purification requirements. These are proposed criteria for a convincing integrated demonstration, not established published completion standards.
completion_criteria.label: Tonne-per-day ethylene or fuel production sustained for thousands of hours

completion_criteria.text: Proposed competitiveness assessment: identify the product and fossil comparator explicitly—for example, ethylene against a specified steam-cracking route, or a named fuel against its relevant incumbent route. Define what counts as beating that comparator in production cost, energy use and carbon performance, and disclose any tradeoffs. Use consistent boundaries that include CO2 sourcing and capture, compression, electricity and heat, water treatment, carbon recovery, separation and equipment replacement. Distinguish measured operating data from assumptions about future electricity prices, plant life, capital costs or scale.
completion_criteria.label: Fossil competitiveness assessed across cost, energy and carbon performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: independently verify the balances and product measurements, and reproduce sustained performance in another run or independently operated installation. Test and report sensitivity to relevant feed impurities, operating conditions and interruptions. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. A tonne-per-day demonstration would be a milestone toward plant-scale competitiveness; additional evidence would be needed to substantiate commercial plant economics and reliable supply.
completion_criteria.label: Independently verified sustained performance reproduced with tested operating limits

completion_criteria.text: A laboratory faradaic efficiency above 80% alone would not satisfy the integrated objective. The supplied ethylene study already reports up to 85%, while its factory economics remain modeled. Selectivity, useful throughput, total energy consumption, carbon recovery, product purification and operating life must therefore be demonstrated together at the claimed system boundary.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated production performance demonstrated jointly at the claimed system boundary

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis: CHM-06, mild nitrogen fixation competitive with Haber–Bosch, and CHM-12, selective methane-to-methanol conversion under mild conditions, are close comparisons because each targets a specific commodity process whose value depends on integrated performance. Their chemical tasks remain distinct: nitrogen fixation activates nitrogen, methane-to-methanol modifies an existing carbon feedstock, and CHM-07 builds multicarbon products from CO2. CHM-13, plastics returned to monomers below virgin-production cost and energy, instead recovers carbon already embodied in materials; it could complement a CO2-derived primary supply.

Roster synthesis: CHM-01, predicting realistic chemical outcomes, and CHM-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request, could aid catalyst discovery and process design for CO2 conversion. CHM-04, on-demand synthesis of arbitrary stable molecules, and CHM-11, predictive functionalization of a chosen unactivated C–H bond, concern broader synthetic choice and selectivity. CHM-07 can succeed for a named commodity without delivering arbitrary synthesis, general reaction prediction or general catalyst design.

Roster synthesis: CHM-03, a manufacturable ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor, and CHM-08, an aviation-relevant rechargeable air-breathing battery, concern electrical infrastructure or energy storage. They could influence the wider energy system supporting chemical production, but neither establishes competitive CO2 conversion. Solar hydrogen, although absent as a separate entry in the supplied roster, is another potential enabling technology; its demonstrated efficiencies do not satisfy CHM-07's carbon-conversion requirements.

Roster synthesis: CHM-09, phase-pure synthesis of arbitrary designed crystalline solids, could support development of catalysts, electrodes or separation materials. CHM-10, positional manufacture of macroscopic atomically specified matter, targets a much broader level of manufacturing control than commodity chemical production requires. CHM-02, open-ended Darwinian evolution in a synthetic chemical system, concerns sustained chemical evolution rather than industrial feedstock supply. These entries retain separate completion conditions even where future methods or materials might overlap.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system worldwide meets the integrated target as of 2026-11-01 remains unassessed by the supplied freshness record.

The supplied account does not establish whether the ethylene selectivity, peak partial current density, long-duration operation and product purification were demonstrated together under one sustained operating condition.
Measured plant-scale production costs, complete energy and carbon balances, equipment life and separation performance sufficient to establish fossil competitiveness are not supplied.
The named commercial comparator, CO2 source, electricity and heat assumptions, and required margins for cost, energy and carbon performance remain to be specified.
The original assertion about complete photovoltaic–electrolyzer–syngas pilot chains remains unsubstantiated within these inputs; this does not establish their absence.
The hydrogen efficiencies cannot be compared directly without harmonizing their heating-value conventions and thermal-energy boundaries.
The tonne-per-day and thousands-of-hours thresholds remain proposed milestones; evidence connecting them to commercial plant economics would still be required.

brief.title: Affordable chemicals from carbon dioxide and water
possible: Factories could make ethylene, an industrial chemical, from carbon dioxide and water using low-carbon energy, at prices competitive with fossil-based production. The complete process would supply a dependable stream of purified material.
why: Chemical producers would gain an alternative source of carbon for an existing product. Captured carbon dioxide could replace fossil feedstocks, changing where the raw material comes from.

sources.who: Liang Huang, Ge Gao, Jiwu Zhao and colleagues
sources.showed: They used electricity to turn pressurized carbon dioxide into ethylene, demonstrated sustained laboratory operation, and purified the product.
sources.quote: enabling stable electrolysis for over 1,500 h
sources.cited_for: The laboratory chemistry, durability and purification steps provide a basis for an alternative ethylene supply.
sources.not_established: The work does not establish competitive factory operation with all these results sustained together.

sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates another approach to producing hydrogen with sunlight.

shown: Huang and colleagues demonstrated laboratory conversion to ethylene lasting more than 1,500 hours. They also demonstrated purification to industrial quality. Factory costs remain projections based on optimistic assumptions.
missing: A complete system has yet to demonstrate affordable conversion, carbon recovery, purification and equipment replacement together.
Measured factory operation has yet to establish competitive costs and complete energy and carbon performance.
Reliable supply has yet to be demonstrated through repeated operation, maintenance and interruptions.

milestones.label: Production sustained for thousands of hours
milestones.explanation: A plant would have to sustain tonne-per-day production of ethylene or a named liquid fuel from carbon dioxide and water, with measured quality and independently checked energy and carbon flows. This would test sustained output.

milestones.label: Competitive costs, energy use and carbon performance
milestones.explanation: An assessment would have to compare a named product with a specified fossil route, counting the whole process and separating measurements from assumptions. This would establish what competitive production actually requires.

milestones.label: Repeated performance with independently checked operating limits
milestones.explanation: Sustained results would have to be independently checked and reproduced, with tests of impurities, changing conditions and interruptions. This would establish the conditions under which production remains dependable.

milestones.label: All production requirements met together
milestones.explanation: A complete system would have to demonstrate product selectivity, throughput, energy use, carbon recovery, purification and equipment life together. This would connect successful chemistry to a working supply process.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether the best ethylene conversion, durability and purification results can be sustained under the same operating conditions.
The fossil comparison route and acceptable tradeoffs between cost, energy use and carbon performance remain unspecified.
Climate benefits depend on the carbon dioxide source, low-carbon energy and what happens when the product is used or discarded.

page.title: Multicarbon chemicals from CO₂ and water at fossil cost parity
page.definition: An integrated process uses CO₂ as its carbon source and water as its hydrogen source to supply a named chemical containing at least two carbon atoms. Its production cost is no greater than its fossil-derived counterpart’s, and its life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions are lower.

goal.need: Global ethylene production was 168 million tonnes in 2020. The National Academies lists ethylene among priority CO₂-derived chemicals and identifies a continuing requirement for carbon-containing products in a net-zero economy. Supplying these products from CO₂ requires forming carbon–carbon bonds using external energy; the carbon feedstock and the energy supply both affect the resulting emissions.

statements.quote: continuing to provide the remaining product services to the economy without relying on fossil carbon feedstocks.
statements.context: The committee describes the transformation required of the carbon-based product system for net-zero emissions.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Carbon Conversion Program
statements.quote: to identify, support, and demonstrate carbon conversion technologies that yield products which are cost-competitive and more sustainable than incumbents.

completion.title: A CO₂-and-water plant supplies a multicarbon chemical at fossil cost parity with lower emissions.
completion.criterion: An integrated operating plant supplies a named multicarbon chemical from CO₂ and water at a levelized production cost no greater than a specified fossil route supplying the same product quality, with lower life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions. Compare equal quantities, location, currency year and accounting boundaries. Include CO₂ sourcing, energy, conversion, carbon recovery, purification, maintenance and equipment replacement. Plant operating data must support the comparison; a prospective factory model alone does not pass.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; operational interpretation of DOE’s published incumbent-comparison goal.
completion.basis: DOE/NETL’s Carbon Conversion programme plan and DE-FOA-0003495, the National Academies’ 2024 carbon-utilization report, and the 2022 electrochemical CO₂ roadmap were searched for a joint commercial pass/fail test covering CO₂, water, multicarbon products and measured fossil-cost parity. None was found. This test gives an operational interpretation of DOE’s incumbent-cost and sustainability goal without adding a throughput or lifetime cutoff.

milestones.title: Laboratory experiments demonstrate CO₂ conversion into a named multicarbon chemical at readiness level 3.
milestones.criterion: Critical conversion functions are physically validated in laboratory experiments (DOE TRL 3). Ethylene: Huang et al., published 28 August 2025, report up to 85% Faradaic efficiency—the fraction of charge forming ethylene—and up to 750 mA cm⁻² ethylene partial current density at 20 bar. Ethanol: Liu et al., published 4 July 2025, report 87.21% Faradaic efficiency and −218.03 mA cm⁻² ethanol partial current density in a gas-diffusion-electrode reactor; measurements in that reactor were performed once.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Assessment Guide, Table 1, TRL 3; generic criterion applied here to chemical conversion.
milestones.threshold_quote: Analytical and experimental critical function and/or characteristic proof of concept

milestones.title: A laboratory CO₂-to-multicarbon system demonstrates that its components work together at readiness level 4.
milestones.criterion: Basic technological components are integrated and experimentally shown to work together in the laboratory (DOE TRL 4). Ethylene: Huang et al. report electrolysis for over 1,500 h at 600 mA cm⁻² and a separate purification proof of concept yielding 99.9% ethylene. Ethanol: Liu et al. report 300 h at −250 mA cm⁻² with ethanol Faradaic efficiency remaining above 70%; electrolyte was replaced every 20 h. These results support laboratory development without establishing a complete plant’s qualification.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Assessment Guide, Table 1, TRL 4; generic integration criterion applied here to the production process.

milestones.title: A pilot CO₂-to-multicarbon system performs all intended functions in a representative environment.
milestones.criterion: An engineering/pilot-scale prototype performs all intended operational functions in a representative environment (DOE TRL 6). DOE’s electrochemical testing target is >20 kWe with cells of at least 500 cm² and at least 2,000 cumulative h using commercially representative stacks and auxiliaries, including on/off cycling and representative feeds. Its thermochemical pilot table specifies >1 tonne CO₂ converted per day and at least 3,000 h. These physical targets apply to their respective routes. Huang et al.’s 100-tonne-per-day ethylene factory is an economic model.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Assessment Guide, Table 1, TRL 6; route-specific physical testing targets in DE-FOA-0003495, Topic Areas 2a and 2b.
milestones.threshold_quote: Engineering/pilot-scale, similar (prototypical) system validation in relevant environment

milestones.title: A CO₂-to-multicarbon prototype operates with its ancillary systems at readiness level 7.
milestones.criterion: A prototype CO₂-to-multicarbon process demonstrates operation in its intended environment, integrated with ancillary systems in a near-production-quality configuration (DOE TRL 7). DOE specifies a system at or near full scale, with most functions available for demonstration and testing.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs), updated 18 August 2026, TRL 7; generic criterion applied to the CO₂-to-product process.
milestones.threshold_quote: System/process prototype demonstration in an operational environment

milestones.title: A full-scale CO₂-to-multicarbon system meets its end-user specifications in operational tests.
milestones.criterion: The complete full-scale process is integrated into its operational environment. All functionality is tested in simulated and operational scenarios and achieves the end-user’s specifications (DOE TRL 8). The system assessed here includes CO₂ and water inputs, conversion, carbon recovery and purified product output. This is the published pre-commercial qualification stage.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs), updated 18 August 2026, TRL 8; generic qualification criterion applied to the complete production process.
milestones.threshold_quote: Actual system/process completed and qualified through test and demonstration

not_found: No report establishing an integrated process meeting milestones m3–m5 and measured fossil-cost parity was identified for either tracked product.
A demonstration maintaining 99.9% ethylene purity throughout the reported electrolysis run of over 1,500 h was not found.
The number of independent replicates of the ethylene durability experiment was not established from the accessible abstract and supplement.
The ethylene paper’s full main text could not be opened; its publisher abstract and supplementary information were accessible.

results.detail: The MEA operated at 700 mA cm⁻² with approximately 76% average ethanol Faradaic efficiency. Electrolyte was replaced every 24 h and the membrane every 48 h; the text does not separately specify the number of long-duration runs.

results.finding: One CO₂-to-ethanol pilot plant produced distilled ethanol at approximately 95% by volume.
results.detail: The pilot integrates water electrolysis, CO₂ hydrogenation and ethanol distillation, but the text does not report a laboratory demonstration or the specified 300-hour electrolysis result.
